name: くもり時々アバロッツ。 (Kumori Tokidoki Abarotz)

claims.text: A Western pastry kitchen producing wheat-flour cakes and tarts; no gluten-free handling or separation is documented, so cross-contact with wheat should be assumed.
Desserts are dairy- and egg-based (cheesecake, tiramisu, cakes); no plant-based or vegan options are documented.
Menu and item descriptions are published on the official site, and one note specifies that the tiramisu does not use mascarpone, suggesting some attention to ingredient detail.

name: くるみの木 一条店 (Kuruminoki Ichijo-ten)

claims.text: Menu and lunch include multiple wheat items (udon, toast, cakes/tarts, doria) and wheat gluten (fu) in the miso soup, in a shared home-style kitchen; no gluten-free prep is documented.
Japanese home-style おばんざい cooking here relies on standard soy sauce (wheat-containing); no tamari/GF soy is mentioned.
The seasonal lunch typically includes meat/fish mains and dairy desserts, and Japanese side dishes commonly use fish dashi, so vegetable dishes are not reliably vegan.
The kitchen is genuinely vegetable-forward and health-minded, using ample seasonal Nara/Yamato vegetables, so vegetarians can usually find vegetable side dishes to enjoy.
Wheat-flour sponge, tart, and cookie items are made throughout the kitchen; no gluten-free handling is documented.
Cakes are made with fresh eggs, milk, and dairy mousse, so cross-contact with animal products is inherent to the menu.

name: 京終駅舎カフェ ハテノミドリ (Kyobate Ekisha Cafe Hateno Midori)

claims.text: The kitchen routinely prepares wheat-based toast, pizza toast, scones and pan gratin, so flour is present in the small open kitchen; no celiac protocols are documented.
Signature items rely on dairy and eggs (custard pudding, cheesecake, rum-milk/yogurt shaved ice, gratin); no separate vegan prep is documented.
Hand-dripped coffee and some teas are served and are likely suitable for plant-based diners, though ingredients should be confirmed with staff.
Wheat udon is the central dish and tempura is fried on site, so wheat is pervasive in the kitchen.
Dishes such as bukkake udon, eggplant dengaku and grilled chicken use Japanese soy-based seasonings, which typically contain wheat.
Udon broth and most sets rely on fish dashi, and sashimi and chicken are prepared in the same kitchen.

name: LUU's BAO（ルーズバオ） (LUU's BAO (Ruuzu Bao))

claims.text: The entire core product line is wheat-based (steamed bao buns and donuts made from organic wheat flour), so the kitchen is a wheat-heavy environment and is not suitable for celiac diners.
The shop is described as 100% plant-based across all sources, so animal-product cross-contact risk is inherently low; no specific cross-contact procedures are documented.
Marked '100% PLANT-BASED' on the storefront and consistently described as a fully vegan bao specialist, so all menu items are plant-based.
Uses additive-free seasonings and rice oil with organic wheat and plant-based fillings.
An udon specialist where the noodles are wheat-based and the dish is wheat-and-dashi-centric; there is no gluten-free preparation, so heavy cross-contact with wheat is inherent.
The broth is a fish-based dashi (bonito/katsuobushi and kelp), so dishes are not vegan and share the same broth.

name: ミアズ ブレッド 本店 (MIA'S BREAD Honten)

claims.text: A wheat-flour artisan bakery where flour is handled and baked throughout the premises; gluten cross-contamination is unavoidable and no gluten-free items exist.
Vegetarian sandwiches are made in the same kitchen as meat and dairy items, and many breads contain dairy or egg; bagels are noted as egg- and butter-free but no fully vegan line is documented.
Genuine vegetarian sandwich choices on the menu, including an All Vegetable sandwich and a cheese-muffin vegetable sandwich, plus egg-and-butter-free bagels.
